exam: A 28‑year‑old HIV patient on zidovudine develops anemia – what PD issue might explain this? — Consider bone marrow suppression due to drug toxicity; check CBC and adjust dose.
A patient on chloroquine for malaria shows QTc prolongation – what is the next step? — Discontinue chloroquine, start a safer antimalarial, monitor ECG.
A child on amoxicillin shows no fever reduction after 48 hrs – what could be wrong? — Possible resistance or sub‑therapeutic dose; reassess dosing and consider alternative antibiotics.
A patient on warfarin has INR 6 – what does this indicate about PD? — Excessive anticoagulant effect; risk of bleeding; reduce dose or stop warfarin.
A patient on fluconazole develops hepatotoxicity – how does PD explain this? — Drug‑induced liver injury due to high drug concentration; monitor LFTs and consider alternative.
A patient on metformin develops lactic acidosis – what PD mechanism is involved? — Metformin accumulation due to impaired renal clearance leading to toxicity.
A patient on antipsychotic shows extrapyramidal symptoms – what PD principle is at play? — Dopamine D2 receptor blockade exceeding therapeutic window; consider dose reduction or switch.
ai.title: Pharmacodynamics in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Pharmacodynamics explains how drugs act on the body: receptor binding, dose‑response curves and therapeutic index. Clinicians use this knowledge to choose agents, anticipate side‑effects and avoid toxicity, especially where laboratory support is limited.

sections.p: Pharmacodynamics (PD) is the study of a drug’s effects on the body, focusing on receptor interaction, the relationship between dose and effect, and the safety margin (therapeutic index).
PD is not staged like a disease, but the therapeutic index (ratio of toxic to therapeutic dose) guides risk assessment. A narrow index signals high risk of toxicity.

Clinically, PD problems manifest as unexpected therapeutic failure or adverse reactions that cannot be explained by PK alone. Common presentations include sudden loss of efficacy, exaggerated side‑effects, or paradoxical responses.
When PD is suspected, focus on tests that reveal receptor status or drug effect rather than concentration.

sections.p: Regular clinical reviews, simple bedside tests (e.g., pulse oximetry, ECG), and patient education reduce PD‑related harm.
Pharmacokinetics (PK) – how the body handles the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion).
Low resource labs may miss subtle PK/PD interactions; a normal serum level does not guarantee therapeutic effect if receptor sensitivity is altered.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe drug toxicity (e.g., seizures, bleeding, arrhythmia)
Unexpected loss of therapeutic effect in infections
